title: How to Rent Hanbok & Explore Seoul Palaces (2026 Guide)
description: Your practical guide to renting hanbok and exploring Seoul's palaces like Gyeongbokgung. Get free entry, find photo spots, and plan your timing.

Your practical guide to renting hanbok and exploring Seoul's palaces like Gyeongbokgung. Get free entry, find photo spots, and plan your timing.

Photo: 서문교 (Korea Tourism Org.) — 서울특별시 종로구 행촌동

Renting Hanbok in Seoul: The Deets

Okay, so you wanna do the whole palace hopping thing in a hanbok? It's iconic, ngl. But like, actually doing it takes a bit more than just showing up. First off, know that most palaces (like Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, etc.) let you in FREE if you're rocking a hanbok. This is the main perk, duh. So, how do you get one? You can rent them all over the place, especially near the major palaces. Don't just pick the first shop you see though. Prices can be wild, anywhere from ₩15,000 to ₩40,000+ for a few hours. It depends on the hanbok quality, how long you rent it for, and sometimes, if it's a weekend or holiday.

Pro tip: Check the rental duration. Some places are like, 2 hours minimum, others are all-day. Decide if you wanna spend half your day in it or just hit up one palace for killer pics. Honestly, 3-4 hours is usually enough for me to get my fill and snap a ton of photos without feeling like I'm going to melt in the summer heat (which, btw, is no joke). Look for shops that offer modern-style hanboks if the super traditional ones feel a bit much. They've got cooler colors and patterns, and honestly, nobody's gonna check if your hanbok is historically accurate to the nanosecond.

Gyeongbokgung Palace: The Main Event

If you only hit up one palace, make it Gyeongbokgung. It's the biggest and most grand. Renting your hanbok near the Anguk Station (Line 3, Exit 1) or Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3, Exit 5) area is super convenient. There are tons of rental shops clustered around these exits. Walk around, compare prices, and check out the actual hanboks. Don't be afraid to ask to see the inside or check the condition. Some shops are way better than others.

Hanbok Rental Logistics: What to Expect

  • Cost: ₩15,000 - ₩40,000+ for 3-4 hours. All-day rentals are more.
  • What's Included: Usually the hanbok top (jeogori) and skirt (chima) or pants (baji). Some might include hair accessories, but often those are extra (₩2,000-₩5,000).
  • Trying On: Most places let you try on a couple before you commit.
  • Hair Styling: Some shops offer basic hair styling (braid, bun) for an extra fee. It's usually pretty simple but adds to the vibe.
  • Lockers: You can usually leave your regular clothes and bags in a locker at the shop while you're out.

Best Photo Spots at Gyeongbokgung

Forget just wandering aimlessly. For the ultimate 'gram, hit these spots:

  • Gyeonghoeru Pavilion: The gorgeous pavilion on the pond. Best light is usually morning or late afternoon. Try to get there before the huge crowds descend.
  • Geunjeongjeon Hall: The main throne hall. Super imposing. Stand on the central path for that epic symmetrical shot.
  • Hyangwonjeong Pavilion: Another beautiful pavilion, slightly smaller and more intimate than Gyeonghoeru.
  • The traditional alleyways nearby: Outside the main palace gates, there are cute streets with hanbok shops that also make for great photos.

Honestly, just exploring the grounds is a vibe. The sheer scale of Gyeongbokgung is unreal when you're dressed up.

Timing Your Palace Visit

Palace hours vary, and they're usually closed one day a week (often Monday or Tuesday). Gyeongbokgung is typically open from 9 AM to 6 PM (last entry an hour before close), but hours change seasonally. Check the official Korea Palace website before you go! Aim to go early, like right when they open, to beat the massive tour groups and get better photos. You can easily spend 3-4 hours exploring, taking pics, and just soaking it all in. It's worth it. Completely worth it.

If you're planning a whole Seoul itinerary and want to make sure you hit all the best spots without the transit headache, you can build this route in the AI planner to include palace visits and curated photo ops.

Beyond Gyeongbokgung: Other Palaces

While Gyeongbokgung is the star, don't sleep on the others:

Changdeokgung Palace & the Secret Garden

This one's a UNESCO World Heritage site and has a different vibe – more integrated with nature. The highlight is the Secret Garden (Huwon), but you *have* to book a guided tour for it, and these sell out FAST. The tours are in Korean and English at specific times. It's gorgeous and feels super serene. Check the hours; it's usually closed on Mondays.

Changgyeonggung Palace

Right next door to Changdeokgung, often visited together. It's smaller but has a lot of history. Plus, fewer crowds usually means a more chill experience.

Deoksugung Palace

Unique because it has both traditional Korean buildings and Western-style architecture. It's also known for its changing of the guard ceremony, which is pretty cool to watch. Located right in the city center near City Hall station.

FAQ

Q. Do I really get free entry to all palaces with hanbok?
A. Pretty much! Major ones like Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, and Gyeonghuigung offer free entry. Always double-check the specific palace's policy just in case.

Q. Where can I rent hanbok besides near Gyeongbokgung?
A. Bukchon Hanok Village also has rental shops, and Changdeokgung has a few nearby too. Anguk Station (Line 3) is your best bet for tons of options before Gyeongbokgung or Changdeokgung.

Q. What's the best time of year for hanbok photos?
A. Spring (cherry blossoms!) and Autumn (fall foliage!) are stunning. Summer can be brutally hot and humid, so go early and stay hydrated. Winter is cold but can be beautiful with snow, if you bundle up!

Q. Can I wear my normal shoes with a hanbok?
A. You wear traditional Korean shoes (kkotsin) or simple sandals with hanbok, usually provided or available for rent. Your regular sneakers won't match the look, and most shops expect you to wear their provided footwear.
